# WattWay — full text corpus

> WattWay is a free, cost-optimized EV road-trip charging planner. Given an origin and destination, it finds the cheapest realistic sequence of charging stops for a specific electric vehicle — using charging-network prices, the driver's memberships, each charger's power and reliability, and the car's real-world range.

Source: https://wattway.net · Reference pricing year: 2026 · Last updated: 2026-08-10

WattWay runs entirely in the browser as a static site: there is no account, no login, and no server that stores user data. Routing, geocoding, and place search come from the Google Maps Platform; charger locations, connector types, power levels, and pricing come from Open Charge Map (a community-edited database). Every number WattWay shows — cost, range, energy used, charge time, number and location of stops, arrival state of charge — is a model-based estimate, not a quote or a measurement. See the legal disclaimer for the full data and accuracy notice.

All figures below are model-based estimates, not quotes. Charge times assume a full-power
stall and a warm battery and are best cases; real sessions commonly run 1.5-2x longer.

## Charging model

- Planning window: charge from 10% to 80% state of charge; the planner goes above 80% only when the next gap requires it.
- Average power below 80%: 85% of the vehicle's nameplate peak kW, capped by the stall's output.
- Average power above 80%: 40% of the below-80% rate.
- Stop scoring: effective price per kWh after memberships, plus a penalty per mile of detour, plus a penalty for stalls under 150 kW.
- Unrecognized operators are priced at $0.45/kWh.

### OUC — $0.20/kWh
URL: https://wattway.net/charging-networks/ouc

Orlando Utilities Commission chargers across central Florida, priced well below commercial networks. Priced here at the daytime tier.

### Tacoma Power — $0.21/kWh
URL: https://wattway.net/charging-networks/tacoma-power

Tacoma's municipal utility network, among the cheapest per-kWh DC fast charging in the country. Priced here at the daytime tier.

### Seattle City Light — $0.32/kWh
URL: https://wattway.net/charging-networks/seattle-city-light

Municipal utility chargers in the Seattle area. Utility-run networks usually undercut commercial operators; WattWay prices the daytime (higher) tier so a plan never overstates the saving.

### Francis Energy — $0.39/kWh
URL: https://wattway.net/charging-networks/francis-energy

A regional operator concentrated in Oklahoma and the surrounding states, built to fill in fast-charging gaps across rural corridors that the national networks skipped. Typically prices below the national average.

### Ionna — $0.39/kWh
URL: https://wattway.net/charging-networks/ionna

The joint venture backed by eight automakers (BMW, GM, Honda, Hyundai, Kia, Mercedes-Benz, Stellantis and Toyota), building high-power "Rechargery" sites with both NACS and CCS cables. Newer and smaller than the incumbents, but priced aggressively.

### Buc-ee's — $0.40/kWh
URL: https://wattway.net/charging-networks/buc-ee-s

Travel-center chargers at Buc-ee's locations across Texas and the Southeast. Notable for road trips because the amenities are genuinely worth the 20 minutes a charge takes.

### Tesla — $0.40/kWh
URL: https://wattway.net/charging-networks/tesla

The Supercharger network — the largest and most reliable DC fast-charging network in North America, and now open to many non-Tesla EVs via NACS adapters and native NACS ports. Rates vary by site and time of day, and a Supercharging Membership cuts roughly $0.10/kWh off the per-session rate.

### Rivian — $0.44/kWh
URL: https://wattway.net/charging-networks/rivian

The Rivian Adventure Network, sited toward outdoor and recreational destinations rather than pure interstate coverage. Rivian has been opening sites to other CCS and NACS vehicles.

### Walmart — $0.47/kWh
URL: https://wattway.net/charging-networks/walmart

Walmart's own in-house fast-charging network, distinct from the Electrify America stalls long sited in Walmart parking lots. It rarely publishes a public rate, so WattWay prices it from reported market rates, which run roughly $0.40-$0.57/kWh.

### ChargePoint — $0.48/kWh
URL: https://wattway.net/charging-networks/chargepoint

Less a single network than a platform: most ChargePoint hardware is owned and priced by the site host, so the rate you pay varies far more site-to-site than on an operator-run network. Coverage is broad but heavily weighted toward Level 2.

### Volta — $0.49/kWh
URL: https://wattway.net/charging-networks/volta

An advertising-subsidized network now owned by Shell, concentrated at retail and grocery sites. Historically known for free Level 2 charging; its DC fast chargers are paid.

### Shell Recharge — $0.52/kWh
URL: https://wattway.net/charging-networks/shell-recharge

Shell's EV charging arm, often co-located with fuel retail. Its Shell Recharge Plus subscription trims roughly $0.07/kWh off the standard rate.

### bp pulse — $0.55/kWh
URL: https://wattway.net/charging-networks/bp-pulse

BP's charging network, expanding through fuel-retail sites and its acquisition of the former AMPLY and TravelCenters of America locations, which puts it on long-haul truck-stop corridors.

### EVgo — $0.55/kWh
URL: https://wattway.net/charging-networks/evgo

One of the older US DC fast-charging networks, concentrated in metro areas and retail lots rather than along rural interstates. Its EVgo Plus subscription lowers the per-kWh rate.

### Electrify America — $0.56/kWh
URL: https://wattway.net/charging-networks/electrify-america

A national CCS network built out of Volkswagen's dieselgate settlement, with heavy coverage along interstate corridors and in retail parking lots. Its Pass+ subscription trades a small monthly fee for a lower per-kWh rate.

### Blink — $0.59/kWh
URL: https://wattway.net/charging-networks/blink

A national operator with a mix of owned and host-owned equipment. Historically among the more expensive per-kWh options, and its DC fast-charging footprint is thinner than its Level 2 footprint.

## Charging memberships

- **Tesla Supercharging Membership** (Tesla): $12.99/month, $0.10/kWh off the per-kWh rate. Break-even at a 55 kWh session: 3 sessions/month.
- **Electrify America Pass+** (Electrify America): $4.00/month, $0.10/kWh off the per-kWh rate. Break-even at a 55 kWh session: 1 sessions/month.
- **EVgo Plus** (EVgo): $6.99/month, $0.10/kWh off the per-kWh rate. Break-even at a 55 kWh session: 2 sessions/month.
- **Shell Recharge Plus** (Shell Recharge): $4.99/month, $0.07/kWh off the per-kWh rate. Break-even at a 55 kWh session: 2 sessions/month.

## Guides

### How Much Does It Cost to Charge an EV on a Road Trip?
URL: https://wattway.net/guides/ev-road-trip-charging-cost

What DC fast charging actually costs per 100 miles, why it runs several times your home electricity rate, the fees that don't show up in the per-kWh price, and the handful of decisions that genuinely lower the bill.

### How WattWay Plans a Cost-Optimized EV Trip
URL: https://wattway.net/guides/how-wattway-plans-your-trip

The full method: how WattWay routes a trip, finds chargers along the corridor, prices each one against your memberships, and picks the cheapest workable sequence of stops — plus every assumption it makes and what it deliberately doesn't model.

### DC Fast Charging Explained: Curves, kW and the 80% Rule
URL: https://wattway.net/guides/dc-fast-charging-explained

Why EV charging slows down as the battery fills, what the kW numbers on a stall actually mean for your car, why road-trip charges stop at 80%, and how preconditioning can halve a winter charging stop.

## Frequently asked questions

The canonical answers live at https://wattway.net/faq. Each vehicle page carries the same questions
answered for that specific car, and each network page for that specific network.
